analysis.one_liner: Strips federal pollution protections from most streams and wetlands nationwide.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing or vote; it died in a House subcommittee, and the 2015 Clean Water Rule it targeted stayed in place until later replaced through the agencies' own rulemaking.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would wipe out the EPA's 2015 Clean Water Rule, which defines which streams and wetlands are covered by the Clean Water Act, and replace it with a much narrower definition written into law. Only navigable waters and year-round connected bodies of water would stay protected; most wetlands, seasonal streams, and drainage channels would lose federal pollution safeguards. The bill never got a committee vote and died at the end of the 115th Congress [S2][S3][S5].
analysis.who_benefits: Land developers, homebuilders, agricultural operators, and energy and mining companies that discharge into or build on small streams and wetlands. Under current law many of them need federal permits before filling a wetland or releasing pollutants into an intermittent stream; this bill would remove that requirement for most of those waters, cutting permitting time and compliance costs [S2][S3].

how_it_helps.text: Declares the EPA-Corps 2015 Clean Water Rule null and void, ending the stricter definition of federally protected waters it established [S2][S3].
Writes a narrow definition of 'navigable waters' into the Clean Water Act itself, covering only waters navigable-in-fact and permanent, continuously flowing waters connected to them [S2][S3].

Excludes wetlands without a continuous surface connection — including prairie potholes, vernal pools, and playa lakes — as well as intermittent and ephemeral channels, and forbids regulators from aggregating scattered wetlands to reach a coverage determination [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: People who drink water sourced from small streams and seasonal waterways, and communities that rely on wetlands to filter pollution, absorb floods, and recharge groundwater. Ephemeral and intermittent streams make up a large share of U.S. stream miles and feed the rivers that supply drinking water; once they fall outside the Clean Water Act, pollutant discharges into them are no longer federally regulated, and downstream users bear the cleanup or health costs. State programs vary widely, so protection would depend on where you live [S2][S3].
analysis.who_pays_short: Downstream water users and the public

drawbacks.text: Removes federal pollution control from seasonal streams and isolated wetlands, allowing discharges into waters that flow into rivers and reservoirs used for drinking water without any federal permit [S2][S3].

Supporters argued the 2015 rule created uncertainty about when a landowner needed a federal permit, and this bill answers that by excluding waters without a continuous surface connection — an honest supporter concedes that this certainty comes at the price of leaving those waters unprotected [S2][S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill delivers a clear, concrete benefit — lower permitting burden and litigation risk for landowners and industry — but its cost is diffuse and long-term: weaker protection for the small waters that feed the nation's drinking water supplies. Because the narrowing is written permanently into statute rather than left to agencies, it would be harder to reverse. A narrower rule was later adopted through the normal regulatory process anyway, so the bill's main effect would have been to lock that outcome in beyond future administrations.

outcome.mechanism: The House committee it was sent to sent it to a subcommittee, held no markup, and the bill died when the 115th Congress ended in January 2019.

narrative.text: Rep. Mac Thornberry introduced the bill on February 28, 2017, with 13 Republican cosponsors, all in the House [S1][S4].
It was referred to the House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee and then to its Water Resources and Environment Subcommittee; no further action was taken for the rest of the Congress [S5].
The bill never received a committee markup, a floor vote, or any action in the Senate, and expired when the Congress ended on January 3, 2019 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: With the bill dead, the 2015 Clean Water Rule remained in effect for the rest of the Congress, so downstream communities kept the broader federal protections for streams and wetlands, while developers, agricultural operations, and energy companies continued to face the permitting costs the bill would have removed.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Downstream communities kept stronger water protections

for.name: Rep. Mac Thornberry
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to nullify the 2015 Clean Water Rule and write the narrow definition of navigable waters into statute [S1][S3].

for.name: 13 House Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; no Democratic cosponsors signed on [S4].

against.name: House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee
against.role: Committee of referral (chaired by Rep. Bill Shuster, R-PA, at the time)
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to its Water Resources and Environment Subcommittee and took no further action; no markup was ever scheduled [S5].

sides.party_line_note: All 14 sponsors and cosponsors were Republicans, with no Democratic support, and the bill never advanced past the subcommittee referral [S4][S5].

industries.note: Builders frequently fill wetlands and small streams during site preparation and would no longer need federal Clean Water Act permits for most of those waters, saving time and cost; the protection those permits provided to downstream water quality disappears with them [S2][S3].

Farm operators would no longer face federal permitting or enforcement over ditches, drainage channels, and prairie pothole wetlands — waters the bill expressly excludes — lowering compliance costs while removing federal oversight of agricultural discharges into waters feeding downstream supplies [S2][S3].

Energy and extraction operations discharging into intermittent streams or building across wetlands would escape federal permitting for most such waters, cutting costs; pollutant loads formerly checked under the rule would go unregulated federally [S2][S3].
